source.title: Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models: Indications of artificial general intelligence or achievement?

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the relationship between model parameter count and benchmark-derived ability scores across a model sample, using a different outcome and method from held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study measures benchmark performance and parameter-count associations, not held-out pretraining loss, token scaling, training compute, or compute-optimal allocations. Its mention of Hoffmann et al. is a cited result, not a result of this study. The reported parameter-count associations are included for V6; the other claim versions are not tested.
record.test_reason: Across 577 heterogeneous Hugging Face LLMs, it estimates how parameter count relates to benchmark-derived ability factor scores. This bears on V6, whether downstream performance improves with scale. The design is cross-sectional and observational, not controlled training runs. No loss, token or compute laws are fitted, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that parameter count is an appreciable positive predictor of general and Gkn/Grw performance (about 25% of AGA variance), with diminishing returns. They attribute the diminishing returns to missing complementary characteristics such as training tokens, citing Hoffmann et al. rather than testing it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cross-sectional correlations and nonlinear regressions on benchmark-derived factor scores across a heterogeneous model sample, rather than controlled training runs and held-out pretraining loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported parameter-score relationship varies by outcome: general ability continues to improve gradually at higher sizes, while Gkn/Grw has essentially no association beyond 45 billion parameters. Pearson and Spearman correlations also differ in magnitude, especially for Gkn/Grw.
record.problems: The analysis is observational and cross-sectional across models with differing training histories and characteristics; the authors state that they lacked data to examine other predictors such as training data, architecture, tokenization, hyperparameters, and fine-tuning. The study also uses a limited, largely verbal benchmark battery and does not test pretraining-loss scaling or out-of-sample prediction.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported parameter-count/benchmark-score results were left out.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No compute budgets or allocation; the Hoffmann et al. point is only cited in discussion.
No comparison of architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes.
Prediction from pretraining loss, out-of-sample or forecast predictability, and scaling within a fixed model family or training recipe; tokens and compute are not measured.
No fitted exponents or comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Parameter–ability associations in the larger n = 1599 and n = 2415 subsamples, reported as highly similar
The LOESS plots exclude models above 80B, since only 10 models exceed it; the top-end trend is therefore unobserved

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is weak for scaling-law purposes. The sample mixes base models, fine-tunes and merges with unknown token counts and training recipes, so parameter count is confounded with everything else. The outcome is a factor score built from leaderboard benchmarks, not loss. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law relationships with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict loss on much larger runs.
Compute budgets and the loss-minimising allocation between parameters and tokens.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.

The study reports cross-sectional associations between parameter count and benchmark-derived ability scores, but does not test out-of-sample prediction, pretraining loss as a predictor, or a fixed training setup.
The study does not fit scaling-law exponents or compare loss-law fitting choices. Its nonlinear benchmark-score associations are not tests of the stated loss-law or compute-optimal-split dependence.

rows.subject: LLMs in the 591-model sample; parameter-count analysis after outlier removal
rows.size_stated: n = 577; mean parameter count = 14.19 billion after excluding two outliers
rows.operation_detail: Correlated parameter count with artificial general ability factor scores.

conditions.value: available for 579 models; two outliers excluded

rows.measure: Pearson correlation between number of parameters and general ability factor scores
rows.note: The authors describe a positive association. This is a cross-sectional benchmark-factor association, not a held-out-loss prediction.

rows.subject: LLMs in the 591-model sample; parameter-count analysis after outlier removal
rows.operation_detail: Correlated parameter count with artificial general ability factor scores.

conditions.value: available for 579 models; two outliers excluded

rows.measure: Spearman correlation between number of parameters and general ability factor scores
rows.note: The authors describe a positive association.
rows.check: The upper CI bound of 0.67 sits oddly far above r = 0.62 relative to the lower bound, but it matches the text, so the value is fine.

rows.subject: LLMs in the 591-model sample; parameter-count analysis after outlier removal
rows.operation_detail: Compared cubic-spline and linear models for parameter count versus general ability factor scores.
rows.measure: Improvement in fit of nonlinear model
rows.value: F(2, 573) = 27.93, p < .001, Δη2 = 0.063; cubic spline fit significantly better
rows.note: The plotted trend is described as a sharp rise from 100 million to approximately 10 billion parameters, stabilization between 10 and 20 billion, then gradual improvement beyond 30 billion up to 80 billion. The authors characterize the gains as diminishing; this is not a power-law fit.
rows.check: The spline-versus-linear F-test only shows curvature in raw parameter count, which V6 does not deny. The partial state rests on the described Fig. 2 curve: steep gains to about 10B, a plateau from 10–20B, then slow gains. Make the curve description the measure, not the F statistic.

rows.subject: LLMs in the 591-model sample; parameter-count analysis after outlier removal
rows.operation_detail: Correlated parameter count with the Gkn/Grw group-level factor scores.

conditions.value: available for 579 models; two outliers excluded

rows.measure: Pearson correlation between number of parameters and Gkn/Grw factor scores
rows.note: The association is positive but substantially smaller than the reported association for general ability.

rows.subject: LLMs in the 591-model sample; parameter-count analysis after outlier removal
rows.operation_detail: Correlated parameter count with the Gkn/Grw group-level factor scores.

conditions.value: available for 579 models; two outliers excluded

rows.measure: Spearman correlation between number of parameters and Gkn/Grw factor scores
rows.note: The rank correlation is larger than the Pearson correlation; the authors report a nonlinear relationship.
rows.check: A rank correlation of 0.42 with a CI excluding zero is a clear monotone association. Partial is better reserved for the Pearson value (R4) and the flat region above 45B (R6).

rows.subject: LLMs in the 591-model sample; parameter-count analysis after outlier removal
rows.operation_detail: Compared cubic-spline and linear models for parameter count versus Gkn/Grw factor scores.
rows.measure: Improvement in fit of nonlinear model
rows.value: F(2, 573) = 87.13, p < .001, Δη2 = 0.230; cubic spline fit significantly better
rows.note: The authors describe a sharp increase up to approximately 10 to 15 billion parameters, fluctuation and slight decline between 10 and 45 billion, and essentially no association beyond 45 billion.
rows.check: As with R3, the F-test alone cannot show the V6 effect. The relevant facts are in Fig. 2: a slight decline from 10–45B and no association beyond 45B for Gkn/Grw.

relationships.condition: General ability (AGA) factor scores across the 577-model sample
relationships.reason: Parameter count correlates positively with AGA (Pearson 0.54, Spearman 0.62), and AGA keeps rising gradually up to 80B (R1, R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: Parameter count correlated with general ability at Pearson 0.54 and Spearman 0.62, with scores continuing to rise gradually up to 80B.

relationships.condition: Gkn/Grw factor and higher parameter ranges in a heterogeneous cross-model sample
relationships.reason: Gkn/Grw has Pearson r = 0.11 and no association beyond 45B. AGA plateaus between 10 and 20B, so parameter count alone is an uneven predictor (R3, R4, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Gkn/Grw had Pearson r=0.11 and no association beyond 45B, while AGA plateaued between 10B and 20B.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: General ability factor scores across the analyzed model sample
reader_labels.reason: Both reported correlations are positive (R1–R2), supporting an association between scale and benchmark-derived general ability in this sample.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Nonlinear score trends and the Gkn/Grw factor
reader_labels.reason: The spline comparisons and described curves show nonlinear gains, diminishing returns, and essentially no Gkn/Grw association above 45 billion parameters; the study does not establish out-of-sample predictability (R3–R6).
